pos: adv. (with a high neck; in the manner of one who carries himself above his fellows)
etymology: From Old French haut, high, from Latin altus. The AV uses it at Micah 2:3 for a Hebrew phrase meaning on high — a carriage of the head and neck that the prophet promises will be brought down by a yoke.
biblical_def:
Micah has just described a class of men who lie awake devising iniquity and rise at daylight to execute it, coveting fields and taking them by violence. The sentence God passes on them is aimed not at their hands but at their posture: Behold, against this family do I devise an evil, from which ye shall not remove your necks; neither shall ye go haughtily: for this time is evil. The word answers itself. They devised; God devises. They would not bow, so a yoke is prepared that the neck cannot be pulled out of, and the walk is corrected by the collar. Haughtiness in Scripture is nearly always located in a part of the body — the neck, the eyes, the look — because it is a thing done with the frame before it is a thing argued in the mind.

The Proverbs state the law of it twice in nearly the same words: Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall, and Before destruction the heart of man is haughty, and before honour is humility. The sequence is fixed and no man has ever got round it. Isaiah extends the same verdict from the individual to the day: The lofty looks of man shall be humbled, and the haughtiness of men shall be bowed down, and the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day. That last clause is the reason for all the rest. The bringing down of haughtiness is not God's dislike of confidence; it is the clearing of the field so that one glory stands where a hundred were competing. David's answer to the whole business is the shortest song in the Psalter and the hardest to sing honestly: LORD, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): proudly; arrogantly; with a high look and a lofty carriage.
webster_full: HAUGHTILY, adv. Proudly; arrogantly; with contempt or disdain.
HAUGHTY, a. Proud and disdainful; having a high opinion of one's self, with some contempt for others; lofty and arrogant.
ARROGANT, a. Assuming; making or having the disposition to make exorbitant claims of rank or estimation.
DISDAIN, n. Contempt; scorn; a passion excited in noble minds by the hatred or detestation of what is mean and dishonorable.
YOKE, n. A piece of timber, hollowed or made curving near each end, and fitted with bows for receiving the necks of oxen.
scriptures: Micah 2:3
Therefore thus saith the LORD; Behold, against this family do I devise an evil, from which ye shall not remove your necks; neither shall ye go haughtily: for this time is evil.
Proverbs 16:18
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
Isaiah 2:11
The lofty looks of man shall be humbled, and the haughtiness of men shall be bowed down, and the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day.
Psalm 131:1
LORD, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty: neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me.
corruption_summary: Haughtiness is repackaged as confidence, presence, or knowing your worth, and the one posture Scripture says God resists is taught as a skill.
corruption_paragraphs: A great deal of modern coaching is the deliberate cultivation of exactly what Micah describes. Carry yourself higher; take up space; project. Some of this is harmless instruction in not cringing, and Scripture has no interest in a Christian who slinks. But the counsel does not stop at not cringing, and the vocabulary gives it away: the goal is to be seen as above, and the means is the neck and the eye. God resisteth the proud — not disapproves of, resists, sets Himself in array against — and He gives grace to the humble. There is no coaching technique that survives that sentence.

The second error is the opposite counterfeit: a studied smallness that is really pride keeping its hand in. Psalm 131 is the corrective for both, and it is remarkable for what it does not say. David does not say he has no gifts or no station; he was the king. He says he does not exercise himself in great matters, in things too high for him — that he has quieted himself as a weaned child. Humility in Scripture is not a low estimate of oneself but a true one, held before God, with the neck free because it is already bowed.
roots_summary: Hebrew rom (H7317), height, loftiness; gobah (H1363), haughtiness of heart; gaon (H1347), pride, excellency.
roots_lines: Hebrew rom (H7317) — height; the phrase at Micah 2:3 is literally to walk on high.
Hebrew gobah (H1363) — elevation, and so haughtiness of heart; used of Uzziah when his heart was lifted up to his destruction.
Hebrew gaon (H1347) — excellency, and in the bad sense arrogance; Isaiah's word for what will be bowed down.
Hebrew tsavvar (H6677) — the neck; the member the yoke is fitted to, and the one haughtiness uses.
Greek huperephanos (G5244) — showing oneself above others; the proud whom God resists in James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5.
usage: “neither shall ye go haughtily: for this time is evil” — the walk corrected by a yoke.
“an haughty spirit before a fall” — the fixed order no man has escaped.
“my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty” — a king's weaned soul.

pos: adv. (from a height; of speech, with the tone of one who answers to nobody)
etymology: From loft, an upper chamber, from Old Norse lopt, air or sky. At Psalm 73:8 it renders a Hebrew phrase meaning from on high — the wicked speak as from an upper storey.
biblical_def:
Asaph is describing the prosperity that nearly overthrew his faith, and the tell is in the voice: They are corrupt, and speak wickedly concerning oppression: they speak loftily. The Hebrew is literally they speak from on high — from an elevation, as men who are not subject to review. The next verse completes the picture and makes its blasphemy plain: They set their mouth against the heavens, and their tongue walketh through the earth. Their mouth is aimed upward at God and their tongue ranges freely below over men, and nothing in their circumstances contradicts them. That is the whole problem of the psalm. Asaph can bear the wicked speaking loftily; what he cannot bear is that they appear to be right.

Verse 17 is the hinge, and it is one of the great turns in the Psalter: Until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end. He does not get a new argument. He gets a new vantage, and from inside the house of God the elevation the wicked were speaking from turns out to be a slippery place. Isaiah's word for the same thing is loftiness, and he puts it under the identical sentence twice in one chapter: the loftiness of man shall be bowed down, and the haughtiness of men shall be made low: and the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day. Height in Scripture is not neutral real estate. There is one place high, and every other elevation is a claim on it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): in a lofty manner; proudly; haughtily; with elevation of tone or of carriage.
webster_full: LOFTILY, adv. On high; in an elevated place; proudly; haughtily; in an elevated or sublime manner.
LOFTY, a. Elevated in place or in condition; proud; haughty; sublime in language or sentiment.
LOFTINESS, n. Height; elevation; pride; haughtiness; sublimity.
OPPRESSION, n. The act of oppressing; cruelty; severity; the imposition of unreasonable burdens.
SANCTUARY, n. A sacred place; particularly among the Israelites, the most retired part of the temple, where the ark was kept.
scriptures: Psalm 73:8
They are corrupt, and speak wickedly concerning oppression: they speak loftily.
Psalm 73:9
They set their mouth against the heavens, and their tongue walketh through the earth.
Psalm 73:17
Until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end.
Isaiah 2:17
And the loftiness of man shall be bowed down, and the haughtiness of men shall be made low: and the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day.
corruption_summary: Psalm 73 is read as a chapter about the believer's feelings; it is a chapter about where he stood when he looked, and the cure is a place, not a mood.
corruption_paragraphs: The most common misuse of Psalm 73 turns it into an exercise in perspective — Asaph felt envious, then he felt better. But Asaph did not talk himself round. He went somewhere: Until I went into the sanctuary of God. The verb is physical and the location is the appointed place of worship, with its altar, its blood, its priest, and its word. The remedy for a believer staggered by the prosperity of men who speak loftily is not introspection but the ordinary means of grace in the ordinary assembly, where the end of all things is preached and the Lord's table shows whose death has settled the account.

There is a second and quieter corruption, which is to envy the lofty voice while condemning it. Asaph confesses that his feet were almost gone, and he is honest about why: he had seen men speak as though they answered to no one and had got away with it. The temptation of the faithful in a loud age is to want that immunity — to be the one who cannot be contradicted. The psalm gives no permission for it and offers something better in its place: Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee. That is a man who has stopped wanting the elevation because he has seen who occupies it.
roots_summary: Hebrew marom (H4791), a high place, from on high; gabhuth (H1365), loftiness; rum (H7311), to be lifted up.
roots_lines: Hebrew marom (H4791) — height, an elevated place; Psalm 73:8 is literally they speak from the height.
Hebrew rum (H7311) — to be high, to lift up; the root behind both the pride condemned and the LORD alone exalted.
Hebrew gabhuth (H1365) — loftiness; Isaiah's noun for what shall be bowed down in that day.
Hebrew miqdash (H4720) — sanctuary; the place Asaph entered and from which he saw their end.
Hebrew acharith (H319) — the latter end, the outcome; what the sanctuary showed him.
usage: “they speak loftily” — a voice with no court above it.
“They set their mouth against the heavens” — the direction of the blasphemy.
“Until I went into the sanctuary of God” — the cure is a place.

pos: adv. (with contempt; of speech, dismissing a man as beneath answer)
etymology: From Latin contemnere, to despise, literally to think slightingly of — con with temnere, to scorn. At Psalm 31:18 it renders Hebrew buz, contempt, standing beside gaavah, pride.
biblical_def:
David's prayer against his slanderers is specific about their manner: Let the lying lips be put to silence; which speak grievous things proudly and contemptuously against the righteous. Two adverbs, and they are not the same sin. Pride is a man asserting his height; contempt is a man denying another's. To speak contemptuously is to refuse the person the dignity of an answer — to treat him not as wrong but as negligible. It is the tone in which no argument is offered, because none is thought to be owed.

What David asks for is not vengeance but silence: let the lying lips be put to silence. And the shelter he asks for is remarkable in its wording: Thou shalt hide them in the secret of thy presence from the pride of man: thou shalt keep them secretly in a pavilion from the strife of tongues. A pavilion is a tent, and the picture is of God setting up a canopy over His people against weather made of words. Solomon adds the diagnosis that ties contempt to its parent sin: Proud and haughty scorner is his name, who dealeth in proud wrath. The scorner is not a category of intellect but of manner, and Proverbs treats him as almost past instruction — reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee. Contempt hardens the one who speaks it faster than it wounds the one it is aimed at.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): in a contemptuous manner; with scorn or disdain; despitefully.
webster_full: CONTEMPTUOUSLY, adv. In a contemptuous manner; with scorn or disdain; despitefully.
CONTEMPT, n. The act of despising; the act of viewing or considering and treating as mean, vile and worthless.
SCORN, n. Extreme contempt; that disdain which springs from a person's opinion of the meanness of an object.
PAVILION, n. A tent; a temporary movable habitation.
GRIEVOUS, a. Heavy; oppressive; burdensome; causing grief or sorrow.
scriptures: Psalm 31:18
Let the lying lips be put to silence; which speak grievous things proudly and contemptuously against the righteous.
Psalm 31:20
Thou shalt hide them in the secret of thy presence from the pride of man: thou shalt keep them secretly in a pavilion from the strife of tongues.
Proverbs 21:24
Proud and haughty scorner is his name, who dealeth in proud wrath.
Psalm 73:8
They are corrupt, and speak wickedly concerning oppression: they speak loftily.
corruption_summary: Contempt has become the standard register of public argument, and a man trained in it loses the ability to be persuaded as surely as he loses the ability to persuade.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant tone of public speech in our moment is not anger but contempt, and the two are not the same. Anger concedes that its object matters; contempt denies it. That is why contempt is so much more corrosive to a marriage, a congregation, or a nation than a quarrel: a quarrel assumes there is someone there to quarrel with. The rewards now run entirely the wrong way, since the contemptuous line travels furthest and the patient answer travels not at all. Proverbs saw where this ends. The scorner is the one class of hearer wisdom gives up on, not because God cannot save him but because he has made himself unteachable — a scorner heareth not rebuke.

The corrective is not a softer tone for its own sake. Scripture is capable of withering language, and the prophets used it. The difference is the object and the aim: Elijah mocked an idol, Paul was sharp with pretension, and neither man was protecting his own standing. What David prays for is not the last word but silence — and what he is given is a pavilion, a shelter in God's presence from the strife of tongues. A believer under contempt is not told to win the exchange. He is told where to stand while it goes on over him.
roots_summary: Hebrew buz (H937), contempt; gaavah (H1346), pride; athaq (H6277), arrogant or grievous speech.
roots_lines: Hebrew buz (H937) — contempt, scorn; the noun rendered contemptuously at Psalm 31:18.
Hebrew athaq (H6277) — forward, arrogant; the grievous things the lying lips speak.
Hebrew gaavah (H1346) — pride, arrogance; the first of the two adverbs, standing before contempt.
Hebrew luts (H3887) — to scorn, to mock; the root of the scorner Proverbs will not reprove.
Hebrew sukkah (H5521) — a booth or pavilion; the shelter God raises against the strife of tongues.
usage: “which speak grievous things proudly and contemptuously” — two sins, not one.
“Proud and haughty scorner is his name” — contempt given a name in Proverbs.
“a pavilion from the strife of tongues” — shelter in weather made of words.

pos: adj. (befitting a lord; magnificent — used once, of the dish in which Jael brought Sisera butter)
etymology: From Old English hlaford, the loaf-ward, the keeper of the bread. At Judges 5:25 it renders Hebrew addir, majestic or noble, describing the vessel — the AV's only use of the adjective.
biblical_def:
Deborah's song slows down over a single domestic detail: He asked water, and she gave him milk; she brought forth butter in a lordly dish. Sisera, captain of nine hundred chariots of iron, asks for water at a tent door and is given better than he asked — curds, in the best vessel in the house. Everything in the line is hospitality, and every bit of it is a trap. The lordly dish is the last courtesy he receives; the next verse has the workman's hammer and the nail. The song is not sentimental about Jael and does not pretend the deed was gentle, but it pronounces her blessed above women, because the man at the tent door was the standing enemy of the covenant people and the LORD had already said He would sell Sisera into the hand of a woman.

The word is worth keeping because of what the New Testament does with the idea behind it. Lordly is the adjective of one who is over, and the apostles forbid it inside the church with unusual sharpness. Peter charges the elders to feed the flock, Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock; our Lord says the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion, but it shall not be so among you. There is a lordly dish in the tent of Jael and there is a lordly manner in the house of God, and Scripture blesses the first and forbids the second.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): becoming a lord; magnificent; hence also proud, haughty, imperious — both senses in the one word.
webster_full: LORDLY, a. Becoming a lord; pertaining to a lord; proud; haughty; imperious; insolent.
LORD, n. A master; a person possessing supreme power and authority; a ruler; a governor.
BUTTER, n. An oily substance obtained from cream or milk by churning.
DISH, n. A broad open vessel, made of various materials, used for serving up meat and various kinds of food at the table.
MAGNIFICENT, a. Grand in appearance; splendid; pompous; displaying greatness of size or extent.
scriptures: Judges 5:25
He asked water, and she gave him milk; she brought forth butter in a lordly dish.
Judges 5:24
Blessed above women shall Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite be, blessed shall she be above women in the tent.
Judges 5:26
She put her hand to the nail, and her right hand to the workmen's hammer; and with the hammer she smote Sisera, she smote off his head, when she had pierced and stricken through his temples.
1 Peter 5:3
Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
corruption_summary: Lordly bearing is the standing temptation of church office, and the New Testament names it directly rather than leaving it to good manners.
corruption_paragraphs: The eldership is the one place in the world where a man is given real authority and told in the same breath that he may not carry it like an authority. Peter's prohibition is blunt — not as being lords over God's heritage — and the reason is given immediately: the flock is God's, not the shepherd's, and the chief Shepherd is coming. Every domineering pastorate in history has been built on a quiet inversion of that sentence. Where the plurality of elders is thinned to one strong man, where the congregation may not question, where the pulpit is used to settle personal scores, the lordly manner has taken hold whatever the constitution says.

The corresponding error is to hear Peter as forbidding authority itself. He does not. He charges the elders to feed, to take the oversight, and he tells the younger to submit themselves to the elder — real office, real rule, real obedience. What is forbidden is the manner of the Gentile princes, who exercise dominion because dominion is what they have. The alternative Peter names is not weakness but example: being ensamples to the flock, a man who leads by going first into the obedience he asks for, which costs a good deal more than issuing it.
roots_summary: Hebrew addir (H117), majestic, noble, excellent; sephel (H5602), a bowl or dish; Greek katakurieuo (G2634), to lord it over.
roots_lines: Hebrew addir (H117) — majestic, noble; used of the LORD Himself in Psalm 8, and here of a bowl.
Hebrew sephel (H5602) — a bowl or basin; the vessel Jael chose for the last courtesy Sisera received.
Hebrew chemah (H2529) — curd, butter; richer than the water he asked for.
Greek katakurieuo (G2634) — to exercise dominion over; forbidden to elders in 1 Peter 5:3.
Greek tupos (G5179) — a pattern, an ensample; the alternative Peter sets against lordly rule.
usage: “she brought forth butter in a lordly dish” — the last courtesy before the hammer.
“Blessed above women shall Jael... be” — the song's verdict on the tent.
“Neither as being lords over God's heritage” — the manner forbidden to elders.

pos: adj. (commanding, overbearing; at Ezekiel 16:30, of a woman whose will drives the transaction)
etymology: From Latin imperiosus, commanding, from imperium, command or empire. At Ezekiel 16:30 it renders Hebrew shallat, to domineer or have mastery — the AV's single use of the adjective.
biblical_def:
Ezekiel 16 is the long allegory of Jerusalem as a foundling girl, washed and clothed and crowned by the LORD, who then spends every gift on her lovers. At the height of the indictment comes a line that sounds almost bewildered: How weak is thine heart, saith the Lord GOD, seeing thou doest all these things, the work of an imperious whorish woman. The two adjectives sit strangely together and are meant to. She is imperious — the Hebrew is the verb for domineering, exercising mastery — and she is weak, and the prophet puts both in one sentence because they are the same condition seen from two sides. Jerusalem commands her idolatry; she builds the high places, she hires the lovers, she pays rather than being paid. And every bit of that mastery is spent on the thing that owns her.

That is the anatomy of the imperious will throughout Scripture, and it is not confined to the allegory. Sodom's iniquity in the same chapter is pride, fulness of bread, and abundance of idleness — a city with the strength to help the poor and needy and the imperiousness not to. The domineering temper always looks like strength and is always evidence of a heart that has been captured by something. Pharaoh hardening himself against the plagues, Nebuchadnezzar walking in the palace of the kingdom, Diotrephes loving to have the preeminence in a little church: each is a will asserting mastery, and each is a man not free.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): commanding; dictatorial; haughty; arrogant; overbearing.
webster_full: IMPERIOUS, a. Commanding; dictatorial; haughty; arrogant; overbearing; domineering.
IMPERIOUSNESS, n. Authority; air of command; arrogance; haughtiness.
DOMINEER, v.i. To rule over with insolence or arbitrary sway; to bluster; to hector.
OVERBEARING, ppr. Bearing down; repressing; subduing; haughty and dogmatical.
IDLENESS, n. Abstinence from labor or employment; the state of a person who is unemployed.
scriptures: Ezekiel 16:30
How weak is thine heart, saith the Lord GOD, seeing thou doest all these things, the work of an imperious whorish woman;
Ezekiel 16:49
Behold, this was the iniquity of thy sister Sodom, pride, fulness of bread, and abundance of idleness was in her and in her daughters, neither did she strengthen the hand of the poor and needy.
3 John 1:9
I wrote unto the church: but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not.
Matthew 20:25
But Jesus called them unto him, and said, Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them.
corruption_summary: Domineering is read as a personality type to be managed rather than a sin to be repented of, and the imperious man is accommodated instead of called.
corruption_paragraphs: The common counsel about a domineering man is that he is strong-willed, driven, a force — language that classifies him rather than confronting him, and quietly excuses a congregation from dealing with him. Ezekiel refuses that. He calls the domineering will the work of a weak heart, which is a diagnosis and not a category. John does the same in a single sentence about a man in a real church: Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not. The apostle does not describe a leadership style. He says he will come and remember the deeds, and he tells the congregation plainly to follow not that which is evil.

The second loss is the reason our Lord gives for forbidding the Gentile manner among His people. It shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister. The reason is not that authority is bad but that the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many. The pattern for every office in the church is the cross, and an imperious bearing in a Christian leader is not merely bad form but a contradiction of the gospel he is paid to preach.
roots_summary: Hebrew shallat (H7980), to domineer, to have mastery; Greek philoproteuo (G5383), to love the first place; katexousiazo (G2715), to exercise authority over.
roots_lines: Hebrew shallat (H7980) — to have mastery, to domineer; the participle behind imperious at Ezekiel 16:30.
Hebrew libbah (H3826) — heart; the weak heart the same verse names in the same breath as the mastery.
Greek philoproteuo (G5383) — to love to be first; used once, of Diotrephes.
Greek katexousiazo (G2715) — to exercise authority upon; the Gentile manner our Lord forbids.
Greek diakonos (G1249) — a servant, a minister; the office He substitutes for greatness.
usage: “the work of an imperious whorish woman” — mastery and weakness in one clause.
“Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence” — the sin with a name and an address.
“the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion” — the pattern forbidden to the church.

pos: n. (hardness or stubbornness of heart; the resolve that will not bend under judgment)
etymology: From Old French estout, bold or proud. At Isaiah 9:9 it renders Hebrew godel, greatness or arrogance of heart — the older English sense of stout as defiant rather than merely thick-set.
biblical_def:
Isaiah has pronounced a judgment on the northern kingdom, and he records how it was received: And all the people shall know, even Ephraim and the inhabitant of Samaria, that say in the pride and stoutness of heart, The bricks are fallen down, but we will build with hewn stones: the sycomores are cut down, but we will change them into cedars. That is one of the most chilling replies in the prophets, and it is a building programme. God has broken the wall and they answer the breach with an upgrade: brick for stone, sycamore for cedar. Not one word of repentance, not one question about why the wall fell. Stoutness of heart is not the refusal to admit the damage; it is the determination to repair it without ever asking who did it.

The word describes a resolve that judgment only stiffens. Isaiah applies the same adjective to the empire God used as His rod: I will punish the fruit of the stout heart of the king of Assyria, and the glory of his high looks — the axe boasting itself against him that heweth with it. Ephraim and Assyria are on opposite sides of the war and identical in heart. The remedy is nowhere in the human material. It is in the promise Ezekiel was given for a people whose hearts had gone to stone: A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh. Stoutness is not argued down. It is replaced.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): boldness; obstinacy; stubbornness; in Scripture, a hard and unyielding temper of heart.
webster_full: STOUTNESS, n. Boldness; fortitude; obstinacy; stubbornness.
STOUT, a. Strong; lusty; bold; intrepid; also, proud; resolute; obstinate.
STOUT-HEARTED, a. Having a brave heart; also, obstinate; unyielding.
SYCAMORE, n. A species of fig-tree, common in Egypt and Palestine, bearing a fruit somewhat resembling the fig.
HEWN, pp. Cut with an edged instrument; chopped; hacked; shaped by cutting.
scriptures: Isaiah 9:9
And all the people shall know, even Ephraim and the inhabitant of Samaria, that say in the pride and stoutness of heart,
Isaiah 9:10
The bricks are fallen down, but we will build with hewn stones: the sycomores are cut down, but we will change them into cedars.
Isaiah 10:12

Wherefore it shall come to pass, that when the Lord hath performed his whole work upon mount Zion and on Jerusalem, I will punish the fruit of the stout heart of the king of Assyria, and the glory of his high looks.
Ezekiel 36:26
A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.
corruption_summary: Resilience is preached as an unqualified virtue, and the rebuilding reflex that Isaiah names as damning is taught as recovery.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 9:10 has become a favourite text at moments of national grief, quoted as defiance and applause — we will build back stronger. In its own place it is a sentence of judgment, the exact words for which the northern kingdom was condemned and afterwards carried into an exile it never returned from. The verse is not resilience. It is a nation reading a providence as a construction problem. There is a resolve that is entirely right, and Scripture praises it — the righteous falleth seven times and riseth up again — but it begins where Ephraim would not: with the question of whose hand broke the wall, and what He meant by it.

What Isaiah exposes is that stubbornness can wear the clothes of every virtue except repentance. A man can be industrious, brave, generous, and stout-hearted against God the whole time, and never be more energetic than when he is rebuilding what judgment took down. The promise that answers this is not better instruction but a transplant: the stony heart taken out and a heart of flesh given. That is monergism stated in surgical terms, and it is why the Reformed doctrine of regeneration is not one emphasis among several but the only hope a stout heart has.
roots_summary: Hebrew godel (H1433), greatness, arrogance; gadal (H1431), to magnify oneself; qasheh (H7186), hard or stiff.
roots_lines: Hebrew godel (H1433) — magnitude, and in the bad sense arrogance; rendered stoutness at Isaiah 9:9.
Hebrew gaavah (H1346) — pride; the first half of the pair, standing before stoutness in the same phrase.
Hebrew qasheh (H7186) — hard, stiff, obstinate; the stiffnecked temper of the wilderness.
Hebrew eben (H68) — stone; the heart Ezekiel promises will be taken out of the flesh.
Hebrew basar (H1320) — flesh; the heart God gives in its place, soft enough to be written on.
usage: “in the pride and stoutness of heart” — the temper Isaiah names before he quotes it.
“The bricks are fallen down, but we will build with hewn stones” — judgment read as a building problem.
“I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh” — the only remedy Scripture offers.

pos: adj. (violent beyond measure; of anger, a flood that overruns its banks)
etymology: From Old French outrage, excess, from Latin ultra, beyond — not from out and rage, though the folk etymology suits the sense. At Proverbs 27:4 it renders Hebrew sheteph, an overflowing or flood.
biblical_def:
Solomon weighs three passions against each other in one line: Wrath is cruel, and anger is outrageous; but who is able to stand before envy? The Hebrew behind outrageous is the word for a flood — anger is an overflowing, water out of its channel. That is the exact nature of the sin. Anger itself is not forbidden; God is angry with the wicked every day, and the Lord Jesus looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts. What Proverbs names is anger that has left its banks, gone beyond its cause, and begun destroying ground it was never sent against.

The rest of the verse is a warning about what lies past it. Wrath is cruel and anger is a flood, and both are survivable; envy is the question nobody can answer. A flood passes. Envy settles in and works for years. Solomon's ranking is a mercy to anyone tempted to think that because he does not rage he is not in danger.

The New Testament gives the fence and the reason together. Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath — a command that permits the emotion and puts a clock on it, and then adds the reason in the next breath: neither give place to the devil. Anger kept overnight is not stored; it ferments, and it becomes a room with a door left open. James states the plain verdict for those who justify their outbursts by the rightness of their cause: the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): violent; furious; exorbitant; exceeding all reasonable bounds.
webster_full: OUTRAGEOUS, a. Violent; furious; exorbitant; excessive; exceeding reason or decency.
OUTRAGE, n. Injurious violence offered to persons or things; excessive abuse; wanton mischief.
WRATH, n. Violent anger; vehement exasperation; indignation.
ENVY, n. Pain, uneasiness, mortification or discontent excited by the sight of another's superiority or success.
CRUEL, a. Disposed to give pain to others; willing or pleased to torment or afflict.
scriptures: Proverbs 27:4
Wrath is cruel, and anger is outrageous; but who is able to stand before envy?
Ephesians 4:26
Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:
James 1:20
For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.
Colossians 3:8
But now ye also put off all these; anger, wrath, malice, blasphemy, filthy communication out of your mouth.
corruption_summary: Outrage has become a currency — rewarded, cultivated, and mistaken for moral seriousness by men whose anger accomplishes nothing God calls righteousness.
corruption_paragraphs: We live in an economy that pays for the passion Proverbs calls a flood. Indignation travels furthest, holds attention longest, and is therefore manufactured deliberately by people who feel very little of it. The effect on those who consume it is a permanent low-grade fury that mistakes itself for conviction, and James settles the question of what such a temper produces: the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God. Not works it imperfectly — works it not. A Christian who is angry all day about things he can do nothing about has been farmed, and the crop is his attention.

The opposite error is equally common in quiet churches: to treat all anger as sin and so to produce a congregation that cannot be moved by what moves God. Scripture will not have it. Our Lord cleansed the temple twice, Paul withstood Peter to the face, and Ephesians commands the emotion before it limits it. The limit is the useful part — a clock, and a reason. Let not the sun go down upon your wrath: neither give place to the devil. Anger that is resolved before nightfall has stayed in its channel; anger carried to bed has begun to flood, and has opened a door to someone who will make use of it.
roots_summary: Hebrew sheteph (H7858), an overflowing flood; chemah (H2534), heat or wrath; qinah (H7068), jealousy or envy.
roots_lines: Hebrew sheteph (H7858) — a flood, an overflowing; the noun behind outrageous, anger past its banks.
Hebrew chemah (H2534) — heat, and so burning wrath; the cruel passion in the first clause.
Hebrew qinah (H7068) — jealousy, envy; the one Solomon says no man can stand before.
Greek orge (G3709) — settled anger, indignation; the word in Ephesians 4:26 and James 1:20.
Greek parorgismos (G3950) — provocation, exasperation; what must not survive the sunset.
usage: “anger is outrageous” — a flood out of its channel.
“who is able to stand before envy?” — the passion past the flood.
“let not the sun go down upon your wrath” — the emotion permitted, and put on a clock.

pos: adj. (having a heart that will not receive the word; unfeeling toward God and toward the poor)
etymology: English hard + heart. At Ezekiel 3:7 it renders a Hebrew phrase meaning strong of heart, paired there with impudent, literally hard of forehead — the two surfaces a prophet has to get through.
biblical_def: God is commissioning Ezekiel and is candid about the reception: But the house of Israel will not hearken unto thee; for they will not hearken unto me: for all the house of Israel are impudent and hardhearted. The clause in the middle is the one that carries the weight. They will not hear the prophet because they will not hear God; the refusal is not a failure of the messenger's technique. Two words describe them, and they name two different surfaces: impudent is literally hard of forehead, the brazen face that will not be shamed, and hardhearted is strong of heart, the interior that will not be moved. God's answer is not to soften the message but to harden the man: Behold, I have made thy face strong against their faces.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): cruel; pitiless; unfeeling; inexorable; destitute of tenderness.
webster_full: HARDHEARTED, a. Cruel; pitiless; merciless; unfeeling; severe; inexorable.
HARDNESS, n. Obduracy; impenitence; confirmed state of wickedness.
HARDEN, v.t. To make hard or more hard; to confirm in wickedness, opposition or obstinacy.
IMPUDENT, a. Shameless; wanting modesty; bold with contempt of others.
OBDURATE, a. Hardened in heart; inflexible; stubborn; harsh; inexorable.
scriptures: Ezekiel 3:7
But the house of Israel will not hearken unto thee; for they will not hearken unto me: for all the house of Israel are impudent and hardhearted.
Deuteronomy 15:7

If there be among you a poor man of one of thy brethren within any of thy gates in thy land which the LORD thy God giveth thee, thou shalt not harden thine heart, nor shut thine hand from thy poor brother:
Mark 10:5
And Jesus answered and said unto them, For the hardness of your heart he wrote you this precept.
Ezekiel 36:26
A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.
corruption_summary: Hardness of heart is treated as a wound to be healed rather than a sin to be repented of, and the one passage where Christ names it is read as compassion for the hard.
corruption_paragraphs: Moses permitted divorce, our Lord says, for the hardness of your heart; and that verse is now regularly read as though hardness were the excusing circumstance. It is the opposite. Jesus is explaining a concession, not commending the condition that made it necessary, and He immediately goes behind Moses to the creation ordinance: from the beginning of the creation God made them male and female, and what therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder. The permission is a tourniquet for a wound the hard heart inflicted. To use the tourniquet as a justification is to read the text backwards.

The second corruption is a narrowing. Hardness in Scripture is not only unbelief under preaching; Deuteronomy uses the same verb for the hand that will not open to a poor brother. Thou shalt not harden thine heart, nor shut thine hand from thy poor brother — heart and hand in the same clause, because a shut hand is a hardened heart in its visible form. Sodom's recorded iniquity was pride, fulness of bread, abundance of idleness, and a hand not strengthened toward the poor and needy. The remedy in both directions is the same and it is not resolve; it is the heart of flesh God promises to give in place of the stone.
roots_summary: Hebrew chazaq (H2389), strong, firm; qasheh (H7186), hard, stiff; Greek sklerokardia (G4641), hardness of heart.
roots_lines: Hebrew chazaq (H2389) — strong, firm; strong of heart is the phrase the AV renders hardhearted.
Hebrew qasheh (H7186) — hard, severe, stiff; the wilderness word for a stiffnecked people.
Hebrew ammats (H553) — to make firm; the verb Deuteronomy forbids toward a poor brother.
Greek sklerokardia (G4641) — hardness of heart; our Lord's word for the condition Moses legislated around.
Greek porosis (G4457) — a callous, a petrifying; the blindness of heart Paul names in Ephesians 4:18.
usage: “all the house of Israel are impudent and hardhearted” — the forehead and the heart together.
“thou shalt not harden thine heart, nor shut thine hand” — the hand as evidence.
“For the hardness of your heart he wrote you this precept” — a concession, not a commendation.

pos: adv. (with hatred; of the treatment Israel's lovers finally give her)
etymology: From Old English hete, hate. At Ezekiel 23:29 it renders Hebrew sinah, hatred — the very word used for what the nations Israel courted will at last show her.
biblical_def:
Ezekiel 23 is the parable of two sisters who gave themselves to the nations, and the judgment on Oholibah is that she gets exactly the lovers she chose, on their terms: And they shall deal with thee hatefully, and shall take away all thy labour, and shall leave thee naked and bare. The point of the verse is the reversal. She courted these nations, painted for their ambassadors, sent messengers after them; and the last transaction is hatred. The world that is flattered while it is being courted is not fond of those who court it, and Scripture says so without softening.

That is the shape of the word elsewhere too. Paul's account of the unregenerate life includes both sides of it in one clause — hateful, and hating one another — the hater is also hate-worthy, and neither half can be repaired by the other. Amnon's hatred of Tamar after the crime was greater than the love wherewith he had loved her; Ahab hated Micaiah for telling him the truth; the world hated Christ because He testified of it that its works were evil. Hatred in Scripture is not merely a strong dislike but a settled disposition against, and the Lord Jesus warns His people to expect it as the ordinary weather of discipleship: If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): with hatred; odiously; in a manner to excite or express hatred.
webster_full: HATEFULLY, adv. Odiously; with hatred; malignantly.
HATEFUL, a. Exciting hatred; odious; detestable; that which fills with hatred.
HATRED, n. Great dislike or aversion; hate; enmity; ill will or malevolence.
MALIGNITY, n. Extreme enmity or evil dispositions of heart toward another; malice.
ENMITY, n. The quality of being an enemy; the opposite of friendship; ill will; hatred.
scriptures: Ezekiel 23:29

And they shall deal with thee hatefully, and shall take away all thy labour, and shall leave thee naked and bare: and the nakedness of thy whoredoms shall be discovered, both thy lewdness and thy whoredoms.
Titus 3:3
For we ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving divers lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another.
Romans 1:29
Being filled with all unrighteousness, fornication, wickedness, covetousness, maliciousness; full of envy, murder, debate, deceit, malignity; whisperers,
Ezekiel 16:49
Behold, this was the iniquity of thy sister Sodom, pride, fulness of bread, and abundance of idleness was in her and in her daughters, neither did she strengthen the hand of the poor and needy.
corruption_summary: Hatred is now defined by offence taken rather than by disposition held, so that faithful speech is called hate and settled malice in the heart escapes the name entirely.
corruption_paragraphs: The word hate has been redefined in public usage to mean speech that causes offence, and the redefinition has two effects, both bad. The first is that plain biblical statement — about sin, about marriage, about the two sexes, about the exclusivity of Christ — is filed as hatred regardless of the temper it was spoken in. The second, and less noticed, is that genuine hatred becomes invisible so long as it is expressed politely. Scripture locates hatred in the heart and lets the Lord read it there: Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer. A man may keep every rule of courtesy and be a murderer by that standard, and a man may state a hard truth in love and be no hater at all.

The believer is bound at both ends. He may not hate — not the neighbour, not the enemy, not the one who uses him despitefully, for whom he is commanded to pray. And he may not soften the truth in order to escape the accusation, since Ezekiel 23 exists precisely to warn a people that courting the world buys nothing but its contempt in the end. Titus gives the humility that keeps this from becoming a posture: we ourselves also were sometimes foolish... hateful, and hating one another. Whatever the Christian now says about the world's hatred, he says as a man who was recently in it and was got out by kindness he did not earn.
roots_summary: Hebrew sinah (H8135), hatred; sane (H8130), to hate; Greek stugetos (G4767), hateful; miseo (G3404), to hate.
roots_lines: Hebrew sinah (H8135) — hatred; the noun used adverbially of how the lovers finally deal with her.
Hebrew sane (H8130) — to hate; the verb of Amnon toward Tamar and of Ahab toward Micaiah.
Greek stugetos (G4767) — hateful, detestable; used once, of what believers formerly were.
Greek miseo (G3404) — to hate, to detest; the world's disposition toward Christ and His own.
Greek echthra (G2189) — enmity; the carnal mind's standing relation to God in Romans 8:7.
usage: “they shall deal with thee hatefully” — the last transaction with the courted world.
“hateful, and hating one another” — both halves of the old life in one clause.
“shall leave thee naked and bare” — what the lovers pay at the end.

pos: adj. (bearing ill will; of words, spoken to injure rather than to inform)
etymology: From Latin malitiosus, wicked, from malus, evil. At 3 John 10 it renders Greek poneros, evil or malignant, describing the words Diotrephes prated against the apostle.
biblical_def:
John's shortest letter contains the New Testament's sharpest portrait of a church bully, and the apostle names him: Wherefore, if I come, I will remember his deeds which he doeth, prating against us with malicious words: and not content therewith, neither doth he himself receive the brethren, and forbiddeth them that would, and casteth them out of the church. The progression is exact and worth tracing, because it is the ordinary career of this sin. First the words — prating, idle talk, malicious; then the refusal of hospitality; then the forbidding of others; and finally excommunication of the faithful by the unfaithful. Malicious words are where it starts, and a congregation that lets them pass at stage one will meet them again at stage four.

The diagnosis behind the deeds is given in the previous verse: Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not. Malice, in Scripture, is rarely a motiveless evil; it is nearly always ambition defending itself. Paul places maliciousness in the Romans 1 catalogue, and Peter commands new believers to lay aside all malice in the same breath as guile and hypocrisy and evil speakings — one machine again, with malice as the disposition that drives the rest. John's counsel to the congregation is plain and unafraid: follow not that which is evil, but that which is good. He does not tell them to keep the peace with a man who is emptying the church.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): harboring ill will or enmity without provocation; proceeding from extreme hatred or ill will.
webster_full: MALICIOUS, a. Harboring ill will or enmity without provocation; malevolent in purpose; malignant in heart.
MALICE, n. Extreme enmity of heart, or malevolence; a disposition to injure others without cause.
PRATE, v.i. To talk much and without weight, or to little purpose; to be loquacious.
MALIGNITY, n. Extreme malevolence; bitter enmity; malice.
PREEMINENCE, n. Superiority in excellence; distinction in something commendable; also, precedence.
scriptures: 3 John 1:10

Wherefore, if I come, I will remember his deeds which he doeth, prating against us with malicious words: and not content therewith, neither doth he himself receive the brethren, and forbiddeth them that would, and casteth them out of the church.
3 John 1:9
I wrote unto the church: but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not.
3 John 1:11
Beloved, follow not that which is evil, but that which is good. He that doeth good is of God: but he that doeth evil hath not seen God.
1 Peter 2:1
Wherefore laying aside all malice, and all guile, and hypocrisies, and envies, and all evil speakings,
corruption_summary: Malice hides behind intention — a man insists he meant no harm, as though ill will were disproved by a claim about his own heart.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard defence against a charge of malice is a statement about the inside: that is not what I meant, I had no ill intent. John does not conduct the case that way. He says he will remember the deeds which he doeth, and he lists them: the prating, the refusal of the brethren, the forbidding, the casting out. A pattern of action is evidence about a heart, and the apostle reasons from the one to the other without apology. This matters pastorally, because a congregation can be held hostage for years by a man whose every individual act is defensible and whose cumulative work is the emptying of the church.

There is no significant progressive redefinition of this word to rebut; the corruption is practical and ancient, and Diotrephes is its permanent portrait. The principle to recover is that the New Testament is willing to name a man. John writes the name down in Scripture, which is a more public rebuke than any church meeting, and he does it in a letter otherwise full of affection for Gaius and commendation for Demetrius. Faithfulness that cannot say a name will not protect a flock, and the love that fills the rest of the epistle is the same love that writes verse ten.
roots_summary: Greek poneros (G4190), evil, malignant; kakia (G2549), malice, ill will; phluareo (G5396), to prate against.
roots_lines: Greek poneros (G4190) — evil, malignant, harmful; the adjective on the words Diotrephes spoke.
Greek phluareo (G5396) — to talk nonsense against, to prate; used once, of the same man.
Greek kakia (G2549) — malice, ill will; the first thing Peter tells the newborn to lay aside.
Greek kakoetheia (G2550) — malignity, the habit of putting the worst construction on things; in the Romans 1 list.
Greek philoproteuo (G5383) — to love the first place; the ambition that drove the malice.
usage: “prating against us with malicious words” — stage one of four.
“casteth them out of the church” — where malicious words arrive if unchecked.
“follow not that which is evil” — the apostle's counsel to the congregation.
